sound.text: Life is Verses is made for late at night. Under opens on high, bright synth chords over quick, steady drums, and Nick Fury takes the same idea somewhere moodier. Then there's 3AM. SyWavy loved The Weeknd's Tell Your Friends and asked Jett2Fly to turn it into a beat he could sing and rap over. For about a year, not much happened. In late 2022, people on TikTok found it, and it's still his most-played song.

inspirations.text: Inspired by Over by Playboi Carti
Built on Tell Your Friends by The Weeknd

notes.title: Cordae
notes.body: Have Mercy is a 2019 song by Cordae, who was dating the tennis star Naomi Osaka at the time. His own girl doesn't play tennis, so the line names Cordae's song and then sets her apart from his.
The album opens quiet: time slipping by and two people who've almost stopped talking. The bragging verse that follows sits on top of that distance.

In the middle of the boasts, one line names police killing Black men without caring whether they can breathe. It came out the year after George Floyd was killed by Minneapolis police, when those words were a protest chant, as they had been after Eric Garner's death in 2014.

notes.title: Leaning Tower of Pisa
notes.body: The bell tower in Pisa, Italy, famous for its tilt. Lean is also a drink, codeine cough syrup mixed with soda, usually poured into a double cup and named for how it makes people slump. So a doubled cup means lean, and the lean has him tilting like the tower.

notes.title: Trevor Ariza
notes.body: The longtime NBA wing known for spotting up in the corner for threes. The corner means one thing on the street and another for Ariza.

notes.title: Keyshia Cole
notes.body: The Oakland R&B singer whose 2005 ballad Love made her a star. He splits her name across the line, last name first.

notes.title: Guinness World Records
notes.body: The yearly book of world records. He's chasing records too, the kind made in a studio.

notes.title: Crème brûlée
notes.body: The French custard dessert with a crackled sugar top. It turns a plain word French: we sounds like oui.

notes.title: Cirque du Soleil
notes.body: The Montreal circus company famous for its acrobats and contortionists. She's that flexible.

notes.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo
notes.body: The Milwaukee Bucks star won his first championship in July 2021, two months before this came out. A chip is slang for a title, which is how Frito-Lay gets into the line.

notes.title: Jrue Holiday
notes.body: The guard who won the 2021 title next to Giannis in Milwaukee. The whole line stays on that Bucks team, from the slang for being honest to his last name.

notes.title: Aladdin
notes.body: Disney's 1992 animated film about a street kid who wins over Princess Jasmine. A friend gets the Aladdin comparison, which leaves him looking for a Jasmine of his own.

notes.title: Catfish
notes.body: The 2010 documentary and MTV series about people who fake who they are online, which made catfishing a verb. The next line keeps the fishing going.

notes.title: Mister Ed
notes.body: The talking horse from the 1960s sitcom Mister Ed. Left on read, he's asking someone to talk to him, the way you'd ask Ed.

notes.title: Nick Fury
notes.body: Samuel L. Jackson's eye-patched spymaster in the Marvel films, the man who brings the Avengers together. He's assembling a team of his own, of a different kind.
Ringing a bell means sounding familiar, and in school the bell rings for dismissal. Either way, he's done listening.

notes.title: Chief Keef
notes.body: The Chicago drill pioneer, whose early single Bang put him on the map. He also sings on a Yeezus song about drinking, which the end of the line points to.
The hook watches her change as she chases views online, and the hurt is that their relationship was private all along. As she goes public, what they had doesn't exist anywhere anyone can see.

notes.title: Fast & Furious
notes.body: The street-racing film series that began in 2001. Its title splits across the line: she's the fast one, and he insists he's not angry.

notes.title: Tyson Fury
notes.body: The British heavyweight and former world champion. Nick Fury turns into Tyson Fury, and he adds right away that he isn't one for fighting.

notes.title: Jit
notes.body: Southern slang for a young guy, heard most in Florida. He uses it for the man who did her wrong.
By the last verse the anger is gone. He won't judge the guy who wronged her, offers to fix things, and says he holds nothing against her.

notes.title: Wagwan
notes.body: Jamaican patois for what's going on, now common slang in London and Toronto too. The intro leans into patois before the verse starts.
He opens the verse by admitting he cheated and calling it part of his growth. It's a confession and a joke on himself in the same breath.

notes.title: Robert Downey Jr.
notes.body: The actor who played Iron Man, whose chest holds a glowing reactor that keeps shrapnel out of his heart. She runs on the same cold machinery.
The hook is the album's late-night center: deep into the night, he's dialing a girl he thought he'd outgrown, one more time. Knowing better and calling anyway is the whole song.

notes.title: Michael Phelps
notes.body: The most decorated Olympian ever, with 28 medals, all in the pool. His name becomes a verb for swimming.

notes.title: Mickey and Minnie Mouse
notes.body: Disney's original couple, together since 1928. She's nowhere near that to him.

notes.title: DJ Envy
notes.body: The New York DJ and co-host of the morning radio show The Breakfast Club. The line spells out the show's name across a date.

notes.title: Under Pressure
notes.body: Queen and David Bowie's 1981 hit. The band's name is what he calls his woman, and the song's title is what she never feels.

notes.title: Otis Redding
notes.body: The Georgia soul singer behind Try a Little Tenderness and (Sittin' On) The Dock of the Bay. That's the bar he sets when he talks about his own singing.
Pulling it off means getting it done, and pulling petals off a flower is the old loves me, loves me not game.

notes.title: Stunna 4 Vegas
notes.body: The North Carolina rapper who came up with DaBaby and signed to his label. Vegas and stunna in one line put his name together backward.

notes.title: Achieva Credit Union
notes.body: The credit union based in Dunedin, near St. Pete. Its name was on the soccer jersey he wore as a kid.
Care and urgent turned around make urgent care, the walk-in clinic.

notes.title: Shundor
notes.body: Bengali for beautiful, and one of the names he calls himself. The rest of the line translates it.

notes.title: Popeye
notes.body: The sailor cartoon who gets his strength from spinach. Strong is slang for potent weed, and spinach stands in for what he's smoking.

notes.title: Mia Khalifa
notes.body: Going M.I.A. means disappearing, and with Khalifa after it the letters spell Mia Khalifa, the internet personality who first got famous for adult films.

notes.title: Friday
notes.body: The 1995 Ice Cube and Chris Tucker comedy, home of the famous goodbye to Felicia. He sends someone off the same way.

notes.title: Yung Miami
notes.body: The City Girls rapper from Miami, whose real first name is Caresha. A Miami trip puts her name and her city in one line.
The hook explains the title. He describes a life written out longhand, then the pen tossed into a fire so nothing gets rewritten. He ends by asking whether that makes it matter to anyone.

notes.title: Marcus Garvey
notes.body: The Jamaican-born leader of the 1920s Back to Africa movement and a lasting symbol of Black pride. He prescribes him for someone who's lost touch with her roots.

notes.title: Two-Face
notes.body: Batman's villain Harvey Dent, the district attorney with half his face scarred. His names are spread across the line in pieces.
The home stretch is the last part of a race or a season, where the work counts most. Pilates is the other kind of stretching, and that's not the one he means.

notes.title: Bazzi
notes.body: The Michigan singer whose 2018 hit Beautiful was remixed with Camila Cabello. He names the song and then the singer.

notes.title: Mashallah
notes.body: Arabic for what God has willed, said to admire something good while giving the credit away. He pairs it with staying humble.

notes.title: Astaghfirullah
notes.body: Arabic for I seek forgiveness from God, said after a mistake. He follows it with an apology to his mother.

notes.title: Inshallah
notes.body: Arabic for if God wills it, said about anything hoped for in the future. He uses it about a future with her.

The verse turns into a letter he keeps restarting until he addresses it to himself, and he catches the dear and deer pun on the way. It ends on a late-night phone call where he let his guard down and nobody heard it.
Sy is SyWavy himself, and a principal runs the school, so he's calling himself the one in charge.

notes.title: Sanjay and Craig
notes.body: The Nickelodeon cartoon about a boy whose best friend is a talking snake. People who keep snakes as friends get the comparison.
The hook is a quiet shrug. He's hurting, she may not be, and they're going to drift apart either way. He says it without anger, which makes it sadder.

notes.title: Lauryn Hill
notes.body: The New Jersey singer and rapper whose 1998 number one single warned men and women about being used for one thing. He cites her twice in this verse as the last word on it.

notes.title: A$AP Rocky
notes.body: The Harlem rapper whose 2013 posse cut is named for New York's 1 train. His crew's name and that song are both here, bent out of the phrase one-track mind.

notes.title: Usain Bolt
notes.body: The Jamaican sprinter, the fastest man ever timed. His name says his ex ran off fast and also sounds like insane, and Bolt comes back as electricity in the next line.
He calls her basic, then turns the word into the military's basic training. He wants no part of either.

notes.title: Chrome Hearts
notes.body: The Los Angeles luxury label known for heavy silver jewelry covered in gothic crosses. He goes for the chunkiest ones.
He tells the breakup in the language of a bad signal. The call cuts out, the line goes choppy, and the affection falls behind like a frozen video feed.

notes.title: Altoids
notes.body: The strong peppermints that come in a tin. Fresh means dressed up and minty at the same time.

notes.title: Jorja Smith
notes.body: The British R&B singer from Walsall, known for her smoky voice and songs like Blue Lights. She's his standard for the woman he wants.

notes.title: Sonder
notes.body: The R&B trio of Brent Faiyaz with producers Dpat and Atu, named for a made-up word about realizing every stranger has a life as full as yours. The name lands at the end of a chain of rhymes.

notes.title: Juice WRLD
notes.body: The Chicago artist known for melodic songs about heartbreak, who died in 2019 at 21. He credits Juice with the idea that something can be a blessing and a burden at once.

He makes clear he means Jorja Smith, not the state, and then gets specific about what he wants, down to help with his hair. An apple-shaped figure becomes a Granny Smith, which loops back to her last name.
Between the boasts he slips in a hard fact: his father wasn't around when he was a kid. It's why he isn't giving up on what he wants.

notes.title: Los Angeles Chargers
notes.body: The NFL team that moved from San Diego to Los Angeles in 2017. LA is a city he hasn't visited, but the team name turns into charging after her.

notes.title: Willy Wonka
notes.body: Roald Dahl's candy maker, played by Gene Wilder in 1971 and Johnny Depp in 2005. He invites her into a candy factory of his own.

notes.title: Don Dada
notes.body: Jamaican slang for the boss of bosses, made famous by dancehall star Super Cat's 1992 album of that name. A cigar in his mouth completes the look.

notes.title: The Notorious B.I.G.
notes.body: The Brooklyn legend whose 1995 hit Big Poppa is named for one of his nicknames. It's the song he puts on to set the mood.

notes.title: Halle Berry
notes.body: The Oscar-winning actress played Storm in the X-Men films, so the storm and her name sit side by side. Her last name also rhymes into the proposal that follows.
